title: Crackles and Deformed Hands / Say the Cause Is Rheumatoid, Not Just Fibrosis

blocks.text: Crackles and Deformed Hands / Say the Cause Is Rheumatoid, Not Just Fibrosis

AMaC MRCP PACES · R2-04 · Physical examination · PACES Station 1, respiratory examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) · Guidelines: NICE NG100 Rheumatoid arthritis in adults: management (published 11 July 2018; last updated 12 October 2020; reviewed 19 November 2024); ACR guideline for the treatment of interstitial lung disease in people with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (2023) · Related AMaC: AMaC interstitial lung disease examination station; this one tests the hands and the drug causes
Mrs Yvonne Garside is 63 and retired from shop work. She has had a dry cough and slowly increasing breathlessness for 18 months. Please examine her respiratory system.
You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Fine bibasal crackles with deformed hands make rheumatoid lung disease. The hands are the diagnosis, and the drugs she takes for them are part of the cause.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates hear crackles, say "pulmonary fibrosis", and never look at the hands. Pass: find hands and crackles together, name rheumatoid lung disease, and list the drug causes. Fail: fibrosis alone, or blaming methotrexate with no evidence.

rows: Begin with the hands: they are the clue, and they also show steroid effects.
"May I look at your hands first? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?"
Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit her at 45 degrees; hands, nails, elbows, forearm skin, face, then the chest.
Link the two: fine crackles that do not clear on coughing, and the joint signs that explain them.
"I'm going to listen from the back. Please breathe deeply, then cough, and I'll listen again."
Expansion; percussion; breath sounds; crackles before and after coughing; check for effusion; nodes; legs; cover her; clean hands.
Say the pair, then the drug question, because the cause may be the treatment.
"Deformed hands with fine bibasal crackles suggest rheumatoid arthritis with lung fibrosis. I'd also check her drugs."
Present in order; diagnosis; drug causes; HRCT and lung function; joint plan; thank her.
Starts without consent; handles painful hands roughly; leaves her exposed.
Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about joint pain before handling, sits her at 45 degrees, covers her afterwards.
Also offers a chaperone, supports her hands during examination, and pauses if she tires.
Listens to the chest only; omits the hands, elbows or crackles after coughing.
Hands, nails, elbows, face, then expansion, percussion and auscultation from the back, listening again after a cough.
Also checks for an effusion, nodes and the legs.
Misses the hands, or reports a wheeze or effusion that is not present.
Finds ulnar deviation with swollen knuckles, elbow nodules, mild clubbing, thin bruised forearm skin, and fine bibasal crackles that persist after coughing.
Also states no wheeze, effusion or cyanosis, and notes reduced expansion.
Calls it pulmonary fibrosis alone, or a chest infection.
Rheumatoid arthritis with interstitial lung disease, and drug causes to consider.
Also names methotrexate and leflunomide, infection and rheumatoid effusion, and says acute onset suggests drug pneumonitis.
High-resolution CT chest, full lung function with transfer factor, and a full drug history.
Also asks for blood tests and a rheumatology and respiratory joint plan.
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): tells her to stop prednisolone abruptly or alone.
Takes no drug decision alone: rheumatology and respiratory agree changes, and steroids are not stopped abruptly.
Also says fever with sudden breathlessness on methotrexate needs same-day assessment, holding methotrexate.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Not used for this station type.

Findings, released as each step is done: thin, mildly breathless on stairs; respiratory rate 18; pulse 80 regular; blood pressure 130/78; SpO2 94% on air; temperature 36.7 °C. Hands: ulnar deviation, swollen knuckles, swan-neck deformity; mild clubbing; thin bruised forearm skin. Elbows: two firm nodules. Face: normal. Trachea central. Expansion mildly reduced; percussion resonant; breath sounds vesicular; fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases, unchanged by coughing; no wheeze or effusion. No nodes. No leg oedema.

Question ladder: 1. What do you see? (B) Rheumatoid hands, fine bibasal crackles. 2. Diagnosis? (D) Rheumatoid arthritis with interstitial lung disease. 3. Drug causes? (D) Told: methotrexate 15 mg weekly and prednisolone 5 mg daily for six years. 4. Investigations? (E) 5. Management? (E)

Curveballs: Three days of fever and sudden breathlessness: same-day assessment for pneumonitis or infection, holding methotrexate. Can she stop prednisolone? Not abruptly. Which scan? High-resolution CT chest.
Cleans hands, introduces self, gains consent and asks about joint pain (G)
Examines the hands, elbows and nails before the chest (A)
Listens again after a cough (A)
Finds ulnar deviation, elbow nodules, mild clubbing and thin bruised skin (B)
Finds fine bibasal crackles, and states no wheeze or effusion (B)
Names rheumatoid arthritis with interstitial lung disease (D)
Lists methotrexate and leflunomide, infection and effusion (D)
Requests high-resolution CT and full lung function (E)
Takes no drug decision alone and does not stop steroids abruptly (E)
Covers her, cleans hands and thanks her (G)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Sit back. [R1 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Listens to the chest only; does not look at the hands.) [R2 Fail] [R3 Fail] It's pulmonary fibrosis. [R4 Fail]
EXAMINER: Plan?
CANDIDATE: Chest X-ray. [R5 Fail] Stop her prednisolone. [R6 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): abrupt steroid withdrawal after six years of prednisolone could cause adrenal crisis. No consent, hands missed, fibrosis named with no cause, and the plan stopped at a chest X-ray.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Mrs Garside, I'm one of the doctors. May I look at your hands first? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, nails, elbows, face; expansion, percussion and auscultation from the back, listening again after a cough.) [R2 Pass]
CANDIDATE: She has ulnar deviation with swollen knuckles, elbow nodules, mild clubbing, thin bruised skin, and fine bibasal crackles that persist after coughing. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Covers her, cleans hands.) Thank you. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Rheumatoid arthritis with interstitial lung disease, and drug causes to consider. [R4 Pass]
EXAMINER: Investigations?
CANDIDATE: High-resolution CT chest, full lung function with transfer factor, and a full drug history. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: Management?
CANDIDATE: Rheumatology and respiratory agree any drug change together; I would not stop her steroid abruptly. [R6 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and complete. Did not name the drugs, the other causes or the acute-onset pathway.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Mrs Garside, may I look at your hands first? Would you like a chaperone? I'll support your hands and stop if you tire. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, nails, elbows, face; both sides from the back, again after a cough; effusion; nodes; legs.) [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: Rheumatoid hands, nodules, clubbing and thin skin. Fine bibasal crackles, reduced expansion; no wheeze, effusion or cyanosis. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: (Covers her, cleans hands, thanks her.) [R1 High]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Rheumatoid interstitial lung disease. Methotrexate or leflunomide, infection and rheumatoid effusion must be considered; acute onset suggests drug pneumonitis. [R4 High]
EXAMINER: Investigations?
CANDIDATE: High-resolution CT, lung function with transfer factor, blood tests and a joint rheumatology and respiratory plan. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: Management?
CANDIDATE: Joint decisions, no abrupt steroid stop. Fever with sudden breathlessness on methotrexate needs same-day assessment, holding the methotrexate. [R6 High]
Examiner note: Added the chaperone offer, repeat listening, effusion check, the named drugs, blood tests and the acute pneumonitis pathway.
R3: Missing the hands. The pairing of joint signs with crackles is the diagnosis, and a chest-only examination cannot reach it.
R4: Saying fibrosis with no cause. A sign is named but not explained, and the drug question never opens.
R5: Chest X-ray alone. It cannot show the pattern of fibrosis or measure the loss of function.
R6: Stopping prednisolone abruptly. After years of steroid this can cause adrenal insufficiency, and a drug decision was made without the specialists.
"Let me look at her hands before I go on."
"The hands and the crackles together suggest rheumatoid lung disease."
"May I summarise what I found and give my diagnosis?"

Rheumatoid arthritis can cause interstitial lung disease, effusions and nodules. Drug causes of lung injury include methotrexate (acute or subacute pneumonitis) and leflunomide; infection is also on the list in immunosuppressed people.

NICE NG100 offers oral methotrexate, leflunomide or sulfasalazine as first-line DMARD monotherapy. The 2023 ACR guideline conditionally recommends against methotrexate and leflunomide as first-line treatment for the lung disease itself; they may still be used for the joint disease.
Long-term prednisolone must not be stopped abruptly because of adrenal suppression.
THINK: Hands and crackles together: rheumatoid lung.
SAY: "Rheumatoid arthritis with interstitial lung disease; drug causes to consider."
DO: Hands first; listen again after a cough.
NUMBERS: Scenario: methotrexate 15 mg weekly, prednisolone 5 mg daily, six years.
TRAP: Fibrosis alone.
FINISH: HRCT, lung function; joint drug decisions.

NICE NG100. Rheumatoid arthritis in adults: management (published 11 July 2018; last updated 12 October 2020; reviewed 19 November 2024). https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng100 Supports: Methotrexate, leflunomide or sulfasalazine as first-line DMARD monotherapy.

American College of Rheumatology. 2023 guideline for the treatment of interstitial lung disease in people with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (2023). https://www.rheumatology.org/Practice-Quality/Clinical-Support/Clinical-Practice-Guidelines/Interstitial-Lung-Disease Supports: Conditional recommendation against methotrexate and leflunomide as first-line treatment of the lung disease.
